title: Longest Self-Adding Subsequence
statement:
You get a strictly increasing array of positive integers arr. A subsequence x₁, x₂, …, xₖ (elements kept in order, not necessarily next to each other) is self-adding if k ≥ 3 and every term from the third on is the sum of the two before it: xᵢ₊₂ = xᵢ + xᵢ₊₁.

Return the length of the longest self-adding subsequence, or 0 if there is none.

examples.why: 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18: each term is the sum of the two before it. 5 and 12 are skipped.
2 + 7 = 9. The first two terms do not have to be next to each other in the array.
No two elements add up to a later one, and a pair alone is not long enough, so the answer is 0, not 2.

hints: Once you pick the first two terms of a self-adding sequence, every later term is forced. How many choices of the first two are there?
For each pair, follow the chain with a hash set of values. That is already fast. Can you reuse work between pairs that share a tail?
Let len[j][k] be the longest self-adding sequence ending with arr[j], arr[k]. The term before arr[j] must be arr[k] − arr[j]; if it exists at index i < j, then len[j][k] = len[i][j] + 1.

explain.intuition:
A self-adding sequence is fixed by its last two terms, read backwards: the one before (b, c) must be c − b. So define len[j][k] as the length of the longest such sequence ending in arr[j], arr[k]. Look up arr[k] − arr[j] in a value-to-index map. If it sits at index i < j, extend: len[j][k] = len[i][j] + 1, where a bare pair counts as 2.

Because the array is increasing, the previous term must also be smaller than arr[j], so a quick check arr[k] − arr[j] < arr[j] skips useless lookups. Filling the table over all pairs is O(n²). The answer is the largest value of at least 3, or 0.
steps: Map every value to its index.
For every pair j < k, compute prev = arr[k] − arr[j].
If prev < arr[j] and prev is in the map at index i, set len[j][k] = len[i][j] + 1 (using 2 when len[i][j] is unset). Otherwise len[j][k] = 2.
Track the best value. Return it if it is at least 3, otherwise 0.
pitfalls: Returning 2 when nothing longer exists. The answer must be 0 in that case.
Accepting prev ≥ arr[j]. The earlier term must come before arr[j], so it must be smaller.
Defining the state by its last element only. Two different predecessors give two different sequences, so the state needs the last two.

solutions.title: Try every starting pair and follow the chain
solutions.idea: Pick the first two terms, then keep looking up their sum in a set. Each chain grows exponentially in value, so it has at most about 45 terms.
solutions.time: O(n² · log M), where M is the largest value

solutions.title: DP on the last two terms
solutions.idea: len[j][k] extends len[i][j] where arr[i] = arr[k] − arr[j]. A value-to-index map finds i in O(1).

followups: The array may now contain duplicates and is not sorted. Which parts of the DP break?
Return the subsequence itself, not just its length.
